E0617.summary: What the rectified circulation makes manifest, turned back toward its Archetypal Source.
E0617.body: Atwood speaks of the operation aiming “to make manifest the Flower of Intellect retrospectively to its Archetypal Source” [IV.2 ¶20]; apparently the fruit of the rectified circulation, directed back to its origin.

E0618.summary: In the Divine Oracle Atwood quotes, the faculty with which the Intelligible must be understood.
E0618.body: Quoted from the Divine Oracle: “There is something Intelligible which it behooves thee to understand with the Flower of thy mind.” [II.4 ¶43]. The passage associates it with an empty mind and a pure turning eye; the text does not define it further.

E0619.summary: Named by Atwood, with Van Helmont, Crollius, Helvetius and Faber, as an intelligent and worthy disciple of Paracelsus.
E0619.body: Atwood lists Fludd among the intelligent, worthy disciples of Paracelsus, alongside Van Helmont, Crollius, Helvetius and Faber [I.1 ¶64]. The book says nothing more about him here.

E0620.summary: In a Hermes passage, the volatile to be drowned while flying and separated from its rust; Atwood reads the images as about the freed spirit and its soul.
E0620.body: Hermes, quoted: “Take the flying volatile and drown it flying” [I.3 ¶16], separating it from its rust. Atwood takes these images to concern the freed spirit and its soul [I.3 ¶16].

E0621.summary: In the Master's words, the substance on which the Fire is poured, so that the Final Cause enters above it and its mortal matter is extracted.
E0621.body: Quoted from the Master: “when thou shalt pour forth thy Fire upon the Foliated Sulphur” [IV.2 ¶14]. The Final Cause then enters above it and its mortal matter is extracted [IV.2 ¶14].

E0622.summary: The source-light in whose evolution the Universal Nature appears white, as all colours united.
E0622.body: Atwood: “just so is the Universal Nature, described as appearing in the evolution of her Fontal Light” [III.2 ¶5]. In that evolution the Universal Nature appears white, all colours united.

E0623.summary: The source-nature which the reflective faculty craves but cannot reach; those who know it by experience truly understand why God is to be feared.
E0623.body: Atwood says that “they only who have become conversant by experience in the Fontal Nature” truly understand why God is to be feared [I.3 n19]. Elsewhere, the reflective faculty is disabled “in the inquiry after that Fontal Nature which, by a necessary criterion, it craves” [II.1 ¶33]. Apparently, then, it is reached by experience rather than by reflection.

E0624.summary: The source from which the individual springs as an outbirth; obscured by the sensual principle and rediscovered in regeneration.
E0624.body: Atwood describes the individual as an outbirth “from that Fontal Reason whence it springs” [III.3 ¶52]. The sensual principle obscures it; in regeneration it is discovered, rising through self-perceivance with creative attributes and powers [III.3 ¶52].

E0625.summary: That whose emancipation produces the First Matter.
E0625.body: Atwood calls the First Matter “an emancipation of the Fontal Source” [III.1 ¶70]; it is not further defined here.

E0626.summary: Nature's source-spirit, distinct from its manifestation and from sensible fire, which is only its excitation or effect.
E0626.body: Atwood distinguishes “the fontal Spirit of nature, apart from its manifestation” [I.2 ¶15] from sensible fire, which is only its excitation or effect.

E0627.summary: The specifying, inward agent that matter lacks; joined to matter it begets a seed. Atwood identifies it with Light and with the sulfurs.
E0627.body:
Atwood treats Form as what specifies a body: subject-matter is withdrawn from inferior Forms, and “one form being expelled, another may be introduced” [I.2 ¶5]. She calls it an error that “the alchemists extracted from the Form out of these metals to transmute and increase with” [I.2 ¶9].

Form is the inward agent: “This agent is the form that matter wanted” [I.2 ¶45]. Joined to matter, it begets a seed. Its identity is stated outright: “This Form is Light” [I.2 ¶45]. One material takes many specific shapes: “though the material is one throughout, forms are diverse” [I.2 ¶46]. Forms are also called sulfurs: “her forms or sulfurs are perplexed” [I.2 ¶48].

In the practice, putrefaction makes the body “to corrupt and to lose its Form” [IV.1 ¶41]. Conversely, the Universal Element's invisible vapor is compressed “into a tangible Form” [IV.1 ¶47].

E0628.summary: The ray of motive Light, which Atwood calls the alone universal principle of increase and perfection: the transmutative ferment and Stone.
E0628.body: Atwood says the chemists tried “to extract the Form of gold” with salt, sulfur, mercury and antimony [I.1 ¶86]. Her own account: “that ray of motive Light, pure, vital, and efficient, we have shown to be the true Form of Gold” [IV.4 ¶9], “the alone universal principle of increase and perfection” [IV.4 ¶9]. When it dominates the circulatory system it is made concrete in life, and it is the transmutative ferment and Stone [IV.4 ¶9].

E0629.summary: The new, concentric, finally immortal form in which the subject is established when it is rectified at the end of the operations.
E0629.body: Atwood says sublimation ends the operations by “establishing her in a new and concentric Form of Light” [II.2 ¶27]. The philosophic matter is finally “rectified into a consummate and immortal Form of Light” [IV.1 ¶46].

E0630.summary: In Rabbi Ben Jochai's words, quoted by Atwood, the Form of man contains all that is in heaven and earth.
E0630.body: Quoted: “The Form of man, says the Rabbi Ben Jochai, contains all that is in the heaven and earth” [II.1 ¶42].

E0631.summary: What true generation would simply represent; Atwood says nothing in nature is generated so as to represent it alone.
E0631.body: Atwood: nothing in nature is generated “simply so as to represent the Formal Agent alone” [III.2 ¶61].

E0632.summary: Matter as perceived in the Night of Matter: obscure, vast and infinite.
E0632.body: The passage reads: “her perception of the Formless Subject is obscure, and vast, and infinite” [III.2 ¶55]. In the same passage the intellect is “sinking into the Abyssal Subject” [III.2 ¶55]; the two may be the same, but no identity is asserted. Who is speaking is unclear.

E0633.summary: In Eirenaeus's verse, a fourfold distilling spring that washes the king and carries him up, also named May-dew and Eve; Atwood's notes speak of a well, not explicitly identified with it.
E0633.body:
Atwood describes the crowned king resting over the fountain and drawing auripigment from it. Her notes speak of a well: “the well is, as the catholic spirit of life, inexhaustible” [I.3 n22], with the occult Causality at its center; another note speaks of the deep well from which the philosophic water is drawn: “because the well is deep out of which it is drawn” [I.3 n36]. The text does not explicitly identify the fountain with the well.

Eirenaeus, quoted: “O crystal fountain! Which with fourfold spring Rubs down the valleys with its pearly drops Distilling” [III.1 ¶69]. The fountain washes the king and carries him up. The same verse names it “This our May-dew which our earth doth move To bring forth fruit, which fruit is perfect gold” and “This is our Eve, whom Adam doth so love” [III.1 ¶69].

E0634.summary: In Maria's words, what the matter in which the science is most easily found contains most evidently.
E0634.body: Maria, quoted: the science is most easily found in “that matter which most evidently contains the four philosophic elements” [I.3 n48].

E0635.summary: The philosophers' name for the vapor into which the body of Light is reduced, which condenses at the top of the vessel and runs down continually.
E0635.body: Atwood: the body of Light is reduced to “a mere vapor, called by the philosophers, on account of its origin, the Four Winds” [III.1 ¶56]. The vapor condenses at the top of the vessel and runs down continually. In the fable, Typhon scatters Osiris's members to the four winds [III.1 ¶56].

E0636.summary: A fourth agent, partaking of the aerial fiery element, that comes over the three fires to complete the work.
E0636.body: In the Adept's account, “the Fourth, partaking of the aerial fiery element, supervenes for the accomplishment o the work” over the three fires [IV.2 ¶11]. Atwood then speaks of “the form of the Fourth in that Burning Fiery Furnace” [IV.2 ¶12], which she says can be conceived only from what is written. The text does not say these are the same, and a Fourth cause also appears at [IV.2 ¶7–8]; how these readings relate is left open.

E0637.summary: Emanated by the Identity after a threefold growth of Light in the Understanding: truthful, godlike, the express image of its motive.
E0637.body:
Jacob Boehme, quoted: “enter I even to the cross in the Fourth Form, there you have Sol and Luna together” [III.1 ¶48]; he does not explain it further.

Atwood: after a threefold growth of Light in the Understanding, the Identity emanates the Fourth Form: “It emanates a Fourth Form, truthful, godlike” [IV.2 ¶18], the express image of its motive. Later she writes: “And the Fourth, as the artist, applies it to the work in the furtherance” [IV.2 ¶32]. The text does not say that this Fourth is the same as the Fourth Form, or as Boehme's.

E0638.summary: A prophesied coming age, the Intellectual reign of Truth and Peace, when the Mother of sciences comes forth and greater things are discovered.
E0638.body: Atwood names the “Fourth Monarchy, which is the Intellectual reign of Truth and Peace” [IV.3 ¶49]. It is the time “when the Mother of sciences will come forth, and greater things be discovered than have been hitherto in the past monarchies of the world” [IV.3 ¶49].

E0639.summary: Author of La Kabbale, ou Philosophie Religieuse des Hebreux, a history of the Kabalah Atwood recommends; her source for the Zohar translations she cites.
E0639.body: Atwood recommends Franck's *La Kabbale, ou Philosophie Religieuse des Hebreux* as a history of the Kabalah, to be read with no less instruction than delight. It is the source of the Zohar translations she cites [III.2 ¶3; III.2 n2; III.2 n3; III.2 n4]. She uses it approvingly, as a supporting source.

E0640.summary: What, Atwood says, the alchemists establish on the same substantial foundation as Greek philosophy.
E0640.body: Atwood: “In just such a foundation do the Alchemists establish their Free masonry” [III.1 ¶3], meaning the same foundation as Greek philosophy. The term is not explained further.

E0641.summary: The spirit released in trance, which can range through its sphere, reveal hidden things and philosophize, though its freedom does not guarantee truth.
E0641.body: Atwood speaks of “the intrinsic intelligence and power of the Free Spirit which can expatiate into the whole circumference of its sphere and reveal hidden things” [II.3 ¶4]. This is the spirit released in trance; it can philosophize, but she warns that its freedom does not guarantee truth [II.3 ¶4].

E0642.summary: Not motiveless choice but the operative power freed from bondage, whose effects follow the will in full accord: the Almighty Magnet.
E0642.body: Atwood: “That was free Will, not the motiveless chimera which human fancy has been prone to coin, but the operative Almighty Magnet” [III.3 ¶71]. Free will is thus the operative power freed from bondage, with effects that follow the will in full accord.

E0643.summary: The liberty, in life, into which souls emerge from Lethe and Egyptian darkness.
E0643.body: Atwood speaks of souls emerging from Lethe and Egyptian darkness into “the glorious liberty of the Freed Will in life” [III.1 ¶70].

E0644.summary: Named by Atwood among the Adepts who compare the work to the Christian Creed.
E0644.body: Atwood lists Freher among the Adepts who compare the work to the Christian Creed [IV.3 ¶27], citing him in support of her own view.

E0645.summary: An anonymous adept Atwood cites for the two principles destroying each other and turning into a Fifth Essence.
E0645.body: Atwood quotes the French adept: “the two dragons do bite one another very cruelly” [III.1 ¶58]. She uses the image to show the two principles destroying each other and turning into a Fifth Essence.

E0646.summary: In Norton's verse, the harder kind of glass, made from clippings of other glasses.
E0646.body: Norton, quoted: “The harder stuffe is called Freton, Of clipping of other glasses it come” [III.4 ¶31].
